chapter: Miles Davis stories and what jazz means
title: Miles's temperament and the press
summary: Gil says Miles is a mix like everyone else and gets bad press for answering dumb questions bluntly.

story.theme_name: Playing with and around Miles Davis
story.community_name: Playing with Miles Davis: joining, sessions and the band

blocks.x: I think that's nice. He'll take you more seriously that way huh? (LAUGHTER). I started to say though, that there's one image of Miles that comes through all of these newspaper stories which always have some negative aspects, and what kind of person would you say he is? Now, for me, I don't know him, I've never met him. Is he fiery, does he have a rather gentle nature? Is he gregarious?
He's all those things. (LAUGHTER). He's like everybody else except that he's, there's a difference in ratio of the various things and when they occur and all that.
Is there a high degree of eccentricity that is observable?
Well what do you mean by eccentricity?
Well I don't know. I just think that's the general picture that one gets from newspapers reports that Miles Davis is quite an eccentric person.
Mostly he had the opportunity and the nature to say what he thinks you know a lot
of times. And many times when he get some bad press it's because somebody has asked him a dumb question. Because you know most, a lot of reporters ask a lot of dumb questions.
Oh that's obvious. All one has to do is watch television.
And when they get out there to a scene where there's really something where somebody with some imagination could ask some meaningful questions they ask these dumb questions, right?
Well when somebody asks Miles one like that he tells them that that's a dumb question. (LAUGHTER). So as a result, he gets bad press.
I myself have a very negative view of newspaper reporters in general. And after hearing the stupid questions that they ask when you are observing them on television.....
Not only that, you wonder how they come up with the articles that they do afterwards based upon the stupid questions that you yourself heard them ask, that's what floors me.
I think the re-write men back in the office must do tremendous jobs sometimes. (LAUGHTER).
Unless these people write their own, they write the articles prejudged and then those questions don't mean anything. I suppose that they do that. They write the same story all their lives.
